4 · One redundancy, six ways of describing it.
If I hadn’t been made redundant, I wouldn’t have started the business.  →  unreal past.

1 · Read the explanation.
Writing about a life that already happened

The three conditionals you need. Unreal now: if + past simple, would + verb. Unreal past: if + past perfect, would have + participle. Mixed, where a past cause still shows: if + past perfect, would + verb — if I hadn’t moved, I would still be there.

Certainty and possibility. Would have claims to know how the other life went; could have and might have do not. In reflective writing the honest choice is usually the weaker one: his life could have been very different.

Regret. Wish + past perfect for the past, wish + past simple for now, if only for the same meanings with more feeling, and should have when you want the blame in the sentence.

Marking a later judgement. In retrospect and with hindsight tell the reader you did not think this at the time. Without them, a sentence like losing my job was a blessing sounds like something you knew on the day, which is almost never true.

Gratitude and closure. Thank goodness I didn’t listen takes a plain past simple, not a conditional. What’s done is done and there is no point crying over spilt milk close a regret rather than examine it — useful, and worth noticing when you reach for them.

The two rules that survive everything. No would in the if clause. No would have immediately after wish about your own past.

The commonest errors at this level
  • If I would have known… — use had known.
  • I wish I would have gone — use had gone.
  • If I hadn’t moved, I wouldn’t have been here now — the result is now, so would not be.
  • Thank goodness I hadn’t listened — plain past simple: didn’t listen.
  • In retrospect I will… — it can only look back.

Two things to watch

1 — Where is the result? If it is visible today, the second half is would + verb, whatever the condition.

2 — How much do you actually know? Would have claims certainty about a life that never happened. In most reflective writing, might have is the truer sentence.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Turning three facts into a reflective sentence

The facts: he was made redundant from an advertising job; he built his own consultancy; he doubts he would have done it otherwise.

Step 1 — reverse the condition. It happened, so the unreal version is past perfect: if he hadn’t been made redundant.

Step 2 — decide where the result sits. The business exists now, but the founding of it is past, so both are available: he wouldn’t have started it (past) or he would still be in that office (now).

Step 3 — choose your level of certainty. He is not sure, so might not have is more honest than would not have.

Step 4 — mark the hindsight. He did not think this at the time, so open with in retrospect. Finished: In retrospect, if he hadn’t been made redundant, he might never have started the business at all.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Everything from the last unit, in one place

Unreal now: If I lived there, I would know. Unreal past: If I hadn’t gone, I wouldn’t have met her. Past cause, present result: If I hadn’t moved, I would still be there. Possibility rather than certainty: His life could have been very different · I might not have had the courage.

Regret about now: I wish I knew. Regret about the past: I wish I hadn’t started. The strongest form: If only I had known. Regret with blame: I should never have started.

Three phrases finish a life story, and they are worth having whole. Gratitude for a past escape: Thank goodness I didn’t listen — note the plain past simple, not a conditional. A later judgement: In retrospect, it was a blessing · With hindsight, I was lucky — both mean you did not think so at the time. Closure: What’s done is done.

Claiming exactly as much as you know

This is the point the whole unit has been building to. His life would have been different claims certainty about a past that never happened — which nobody can have. His life could have been different claims only that it was possible. I might not have had the courage is the honest version of I wouldn’t have had the courage. In a personal essay, the hedged version reads as self-knowledge and the certain one reads as posturing.

The same choice runs through the regrets. I wish I hadn’t started is regret; I should never have started adds blame; Thank goodness I didn’t reverses the judgement entirely. A good closing paragraph usually moves through more than one of these rather than staying on one note.

Errors to watch: If I wouldn’t have gone → If I hadn’t gone · If I hadn’t moved, I would have still been there now → would still be · Thank goodness I hadn’t listened → I didn’t listen · In retrospective → in retrospect.

Stage 5 · Speaking & WritingWriting

A short biography

The last piece of writing in the course: somebody’s life in four paragraphs, with the turning points marked and not smoothed over.

The brief

Write a short biography of somebody you know well — a relative, a colleague, a friend, or yourself. Give the background, the turning point, what followed, and what the standard version of the story leaves out. Mark every hindsight judgement as hindsight, and use might have wherever you cannot honestly claim to know.

1 · Make notes before you speak. One line each.
1Who, and their background in one line:
2The turning point, and whether it was chosen:
3What followed from it:
4What would be different now without it:

2 · Take the two roles, then swap.
Useful language
  • She came from a… background, and it was not an ideal start.
  • If she hadn’t…, she would still be…
  • In retrospect… · With hindsight…
  • The stereotype is…; what actually happened was…
Partner AYou · the biographer
  • Background first, in two sentences.
  • One turning point, and say whether it was chosen.
  • Follow it forward to today.
  • Say what the tidy version leaves out.
Partner BYour teacher · the editor
  • Ask what else could have followed from that point.
  • Challenge every claim about a life that did not happen.
  • Ask which parts the person would dispute.
  • Catch any would in an if clause.

1 · Read the model.
Model · a life in four paragraphs

My grandmother was born in 1938 into a background that decided almost everything about the next twenty years: a run-down street, a father who was away, and a school she left at fourteen because the family needed the wage. She threw the javelin for the county at sixteen, which is the one fact everybody knows about her, and she mentions it about once a decade.

The turning point was not chosen. The factory closed in 1961 and she took the only work available, which was in an office, and which required her to learn to type in three weeks. If the factory hadn’t closed, she would have stayed on that line until it shut anyway, twelve years later, and she might never have sat an examination in her life. As it was, she took two, at night, and ran the wages department for nineteen years.

The consequences are still visible. If she hadn’t moved into that office, she would not now own the property she lives in; the mortgage was possible only on the second salary, and the street stopped being affordable about ten years after she bought. Her sister, who stayed in the same industry, rents. Neither of them thinks this is a story about merit, and neither of them frets about it either.

What the tidy version leaves out is how long it took to look like good news. In retrospect the closure was the best thing that happened to her; at the time it was three months of genuine fear, and she has never once described it as an opportunity. The stereotype of the determined working-class woman who seized her chance is almost true, and she would object to every word of it.
